_note: Written by hand before any model was run against this data. The point of the ordering is that our judgement is the benchmark and the agent is scored against it — not the reverse. `acceptable_offer_ids` is a band rather than one id because more than one offer can be defensible; `preferred_offer_id` is the call we'd make ourselves.
_principles: Offer strength tracks how unlikely the fan was to return unaided. Never cart value, never loyalty.

Take the cheapest tool that could plausibly work — and price every tool honestly. A free upgrade is not free: it hands over a seat someone else would likely have bought and only gives back the cheaper one it frees. Moving a fan from a $35 seat to a $53 one costs $18 a seat, which makes upgrades the expensive option rather than the thrifty one.
A discount costs its full face value in margin, because a ticket is perishable and the marginal cost of one more person in a seat is close to nothing.

The cooling-off window is about money, not silence. Under 24 hours a fan may hear from us, but only in a way that costs nothing; under 2 hours they hear nothing at all, because they may still be at the checkout.

C-1001.why: Left 3 hours ago by a regular who bought 21 days ago — the likeliest fan here to finish on their own, so nothing that costs money should go near them. But a reminder costs nothing, and someone who walked away from a half-finished purchase this recently most likely got interrupted rather than changed their mind. The cooling-off window doesn't block contact, it caps what contact may cost: reminder, and nothing dearer, until tomorrow.

C-1002.why: Never purchased, so there is genuinely no history saying he comes back — the one cart in the set where a real offer is honest rather than lazy. Four seats of a brand new fan is the highest acquisition value here, and 15% of $140 is $21. An upgrade for four would give up roughly $77 of expected ticket revenue, so the deepest discount we sell is still the cheaper way to win him.

C-1003.why: Has not opted in to email. There is no channel, so there is no decision to make. This never reaches a model — it's a rule, not a judgement, and it should be visible on screen rather than silently dropped.

C-1004.why: The trap in this dataset. Biggest cart on the page at $540, and the strongest instinct is to chase it — but it was abandoned one hour ago by a fan with 40 lifetime tickets who bought nine days ago. He is the likeliest person here to finish on his own, and a discount to the club's most loyal fan is both wasted margin and slightly insulting. Hold. If it's still open tomorrow, a reminder — never cash.

C-1005.why: One ticket, 300 days ago, cart cold for four days. The relationship is already gone, so the unaided return chance is near zero and a real offer is justified. A 10% discount costs $7. The upgrade is the tempting answer because it costs no cash — but moving two seats from Upper Deck to Lower Bowl gives up about $38 of expected ticket revenue, five times the discount. Cheapest tool that plausibly works means the money, not the seats.
